title: Recombination-assisted megaprimer (RAM) cloning
author: Mathieu, Alvarez, et al.
materials: For laboratories performing low-throughput cloning of single gene insertions, RF cloning offers a simple, cheap, and mostly effective method for rapid DNA manipulations. However, when RF cloning fails, researchers are often required to utilize completely different cloning methods that require additional design and reagents, and that are often time-consuming. RAM cloning saves time and resources by allowing researchers to utilize the same megaprimer which was produced for RF cloning, and requires only one new primer. Furthermore we found RAM cloning to be more reliable than any other cloning method we have utilized. Our experience suggests that it is not hindered by insert sizes up to at least 2460 bp (maximum size assessed) or GC content up to at least 72% (Table 1). Furthermore, while RF cloning may be less expensive per reaction based on reagent costs, we found that in many cases it would have been more economical to utilize RAM cloning over RF cloning due to the increased amount of screening we have had to perform for some cloning reactions.

steps.title: Megaprimer synthesis
steps.instruction: Generate the megaprimer by designing primers, amplifying the insert, verifying size, purifying, and measuring concentration.

substeps.instruction: If RAM cloning follows a failed RF‑cloning attempt, reuse the previously produced megaprimer and skip primer design; otherwise design a forward primer (MF) that adds the 20 bp sequence immediately upstream of the insertion site and a reverse primer (MR) that adds the reverse‑complement of the 20 bp sequence immediately downstream of the insertion site, keeping each primer ≤40 bp in length.

Set up a 25 µL PCR with 12.5 µL 2× Kapa HiFi HotStart ReadyMix, 0.4 µM MF, 0.4 µM MR, 10–50 ng DNA template, and nuclease‑free water to volume. Cycle: 35 s at 98 °C; 15–20 cycles of 35 s at 95 °C, 35 s annealing at the average megaprimer Tm, 30 s/kbp extension at 72 °C; finish with 5 min at 72 °C.
Add 5 µL of 6× loading dye directly to the PCR mix, run the product on a 1 % agarose gel, and gel‑extract the band corresponding to the megaprimer.
Determine the megaprimer concentration by UV absorbance.

steps.title: Cloning PCR and DpnI digestion
steps.instruction: Fuse the megaprimer to the target vector by a secondary PCR, then remove parental plasmid with DpnI.

substeps.instruction: Design the CR primer: its 5′ end contains a 20‑bp overlap complementary to the 5′ region of the MF primer (upstream of the insertion site); the remainder matches the plasmid sequence upstream of that region.

Prepare a 25 µL fusion PCR containing 12.5 µL Kapa HiFi HotStart ReadyMix, 0.4 µM MF, 0.4 µM CR, 10 ng target plasmid, megaprimer at a 20:1 molar excess relative to plasmid, 1 M betaine, and water to volume. Cycle: 35 s at 98 °C; 5–15 cycles of 35 s at 95 °C, 35 s annealing at 45 °C, 30 s/kbp extension at 72 °C; final 5 min at 72 °C.
Add 2 µL DpnI (20 U) directly to the PCR tube, incubate at 37 °C for 2 h, then heat‑inactivate at 80 °C for 20 min.

steps.title: Transformation into E. coli
steps.instruction: Introduce the linearized, DpnI‑treated product into chemically competent cells and recover transformants.

substeps.instruction: Mix 3 µL of the DpnI‑treated PCR reaction with 50 µL chemically competent E. coli cloning‑grade cells; incubate on ice for 10–15 min.
Heat‑shock at 42 °C for 30 s, then return to ice for 1 min.
Add 750 µL recovery medium, shake at 37 °C for 1 h.
Centrifuge at maximum speed for 30 s, carefully remove 150 µL of the supernatant (retain), discard the remainder, and resuspend the cell pellet in the retained 150 µL.
Plate the resuspended cells on 1 % agar plates containing the appropriate antibiotic and incubate overnight at 37 °C.

steps.title: Colony PCR and sequencing
steps.instruction: Screen colonies for correct insertion and confirm sequence.

substeps.instruction: Set up 4–6 colony‑PCR reactions (25 µL each) containing 12.5 µL Kapa HiFi HotStart ReadyMix, 0.4 µM forward sequencing primer, 0.4 µM reverse sequencing primer, and nuclease‑free water to volume.
Using a sterile toothpick or pipette tip, pick an individual colony, dip the tip into a PCR tube, then streak the same tip onto a fresh antibiotic plate; incubate the plate overnight at 37 °C.
Run PCR with the following program: 35 s at 98 °C; 30 cycles of 35 s at 95 °C, 35 s annealing at the average primer Tm, 30 s/kbp extension at 72 °C; final 5 min at 72 °C.

Add 5 µL 6× loading dye to the entire PCR volume, run the products on a 1 % agarose gel, extract the band of the expected size, measure DNA concentration by UV spectroscopy, and submit the purified product for Sanger sequencing.

description: RAM cloning is designed to work as either a stand-alone method, or as a means to salvage a failed restriction-free (RF)-cloning attempt. Both RAM and RF-cloning involve the following steps: (i) the synthesis of a megaprimer; (ii) cloning of the megaprimer into the target vector; (iii) removal of parental plasmid from the reaction; (iv) transformation of target organism; and (v) verification of proper insertion. RAM cloning differs from RF-cloning in that it incorporates and additional primer to turn the linear amplification step into an exponential amplification. Additionally, RAM cloning utilizes homologous recombination for end-joining.
